title: A logic error in detect_proxy caused truncation of environment variable names for long protocol schemes.
excerpt:
In lib/url.c, the detect_proxy function uses a fixed-size buffer, proxy_env[20], to construct proxy environment variable names (e.g., http_proxy). However, the curl URL parser (lib/urlapi.c) allows protocol schemes up to 40 characters (MAX_SCHEME_LEN). When a protocol scheme longer than 12 characters is used, the environment variable name is silently truncated to 19 characters by curl_msnprintf. This causes a business logic error where curl may read configuration from an unintended (truncated) environment variable, causing potentially unexpected proxy behavior in applications using custom schemes.

Google Gemini AI was used as an analysis aid only; all findings, including the truncation behavior, were manually verified by reviewing the source code and testing a PoC.

Affected Versions
- curl 8.18.0-DEV (latest master branch)
- Platform: Windows 10 x64 (platform-independent logic issue)

Steps to Reproduce
1. Inspect lib/url.c lines 2060–2067.
2. Note that proxy_env is declared as char proxy_env[20];.
3. Observe that conn->handler->scheme can be up to 40 characters (MAX_SCHEME_LEN).
4. Call curl_msnprintf(proxy_env, sizeof(proxy_env), "%s_proxy", conn->handler->scheme); with a long scheme.
5. Example: "extremelylongprotocolname" (25 characters) will be truncated to "extremelylongsc" instead of "extremelylongprotocolname_proxy".

Supporting/Reference Materials
- Source code snippet from lib/url.c (lines 2060–2067)
- PoC code (poc_truncation.c) demonstrating truncation
- Screenshot of PoC execution showing truncation
- Screenshot of the vulnerable code in lib/url.c

## Impact

A business logic flaw allows proxy configuration manipulation or bypass through truncating environment variable names. This can lead to unexpected network behavior or bypass security policies that rely on protocol-specific proxy settings. An attacker with control over environment variables could set truncated variable names to redirect traffic through an unauthorized proxy.
explain: The code does what the report says, but curl's own policy may exclude it. A maintainer decides.

claims.text: when a protocol scheme longer than 12 characters is used, the environment variable name is silently truncated
claims.reasoning: The buffer is 20 bytes; the format "%s_proxy" adds 6 characters ("_proxy") plus a null terminator, so any scheme longer than 13 characters will be silently truncated by curl_msnprintf. The report's "12 characters" is approximately correct.

claims.reasoning: After truncation, `curl_getenv(proxy_env)` at line 2070 reads the truncated name, so curl may look up an unintended environment variable.

claims.reasoning: The truncation behavior is real. The example "extremelylongprotocolname" (25 chars) would be truncated to the first 19 characters of the formatted string (e.g., "extremelylongprotocol") rather than "extremelylongsc" as the report states, but the core claim of silent truncation is correct.

key_reasons: The truncation behavior described in the report is real: the 20-byte buffer cannot hold scheme names longer than ~13 characters plus the "_proxy" suffix, so longer schemes are silently truncated.

However, exploitation requires an attacker who can control environment variables on the local system. The report explicitly states: "An attacker with control over environment variables could set truncated variable names to redirect traffic."

The project's security policy lists "Local attackers already present" as a category that is not considered a security problem: "When an issue can only be attacked or misused by an attacker present on the local system or network, the bar is raised. If a local user wrongfully has elevated rights on your system enough to attack curl, they can probably already do much worse harm and the problem is not really in curl."

Standard protocol schemes (http, https, ftp, etc.) are well under the 13-character limit, so the truncation only affects unusual custom schemes. The code comment at lines 2072–2083 shows the developers already consider environment-variable manipulation in webserver contexts a known risk and mitigate it for HTTP_PROXY.
reply:
Thank you for the detailed analysis. The truncation you identified is real: the 20-byte buffer in detect_proxy() cannot accommodate scheme names longer than about 13 characters, so longer custom schemes are silently truncated when forming the environment variable name.

However, this is not considered a security vulnerability in curl because exploitation requires an attacker who can already set environment variables on the local system. Our security policy explicitly states that issues requiring a local attacker "raise the bar" and are not treated as curl security problems, since such an attacker can likely cause far worse harm. Standard schemes (http, https, ftp, etc.) are unaffected.

If you have a scenario where this truncation can be triggered without local environment-variable control, please share those details.
